claims.text: The starting Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles are homogeneous, single-phase solid solutions.
Cooling rate modulates the premelting and melting behavior of Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles.
Slower cooling permits more extensive atomic diffusion than rapid cooling.
Cu is a lower-melting constituent of the Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticle.
Cu has relatively high surface mobility in this alloy system.
Element-specific surface diffusion causes local compositional rearrangement and transient surface segregation.
Diffusion-induced compositional fluctuations broaden the premelting transition.
Diffusion-induced compositional fluctuations shift the premelting transition relative to simpler nanoparticles.
Localized compositional nonuniformities delay the onset of melting.
Single-metal or bimetallic nanoparticles melt more uniformly than the proposed HEA nanoparticles.
Single-metal or bimetallic nanoparticles have lower melting-transition temperatures than the proposed HEA nanoparticles.
Slower cooling will produce a higher melting-onset temperature in the HEA nanoparticles than in baseline single-metal or bimetallic nanoparticles.
Slower cooling will produce a broader premelting regime in the HEA nanoparticles than in baseline particles.
The HEA transition will be more gradual and spatially variable than the transition in baseline particles.
Cooling-rate variation can significantly alter the microstructure and phases obtained in high-entropy alloys.
Rapid cooling can crystallize related five-element alloy nanoparticles without element segregation or phase separation.
Particle size, defect density, and precursor history may also affect the thermal transition.
The proposed scope is limited to homogeneous single-phase nanoparticles under inert conditions near the premelting and melting regime with controlled cooling rates.
Single-metal or bimetallic particles prepared and tested under identical conditions provide the experimental control.
Absence of both cooling-rate-dependent transition changes and slower-cooling-induced compositional inhomogeneity would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention heats particles into or above the premelting regime and only then varies the cooling rate, but the predicted and measured outcome is described as the onset of melting. A subsequent cooling rate cannot alter a melting onset that already occurred during heating unless a prior thermal-cycle history is explicitly introduced; on cooling, the corresponding transition would be solidification rather than melting.
